patient.chief_complaint: One-week fever with confusion, inability to walk, and ascending paralysis — initially presenting as meningoencephalitis, with progressive neurological deterioration requiring intubation.
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. G. is a 67-year-old woman presenting with a 1-week history of intermittent fever. Three days before this admission, she was seen in the emergency department for presumed community-acquired pneumonia and treated with levofloxacin. She returned 3 days later with worsening fever (101°F), generalized weakness, inability to walk, confusion, and difficulty expressing herself. She denied sick contacts, new travel, or animal exposures. On exam: crackles in right middle and lower lung fields. Chest X-ray showed patchy left lower lobe density. She was started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin for suspected community-acquired pneumonia. Neurological assessment on admission showed mild confusion oriented to person, time, and place, with weakness but still able to move extremities — she could not lift her arms more than 10 inches. A head CT was unremarkable. The following day she was oriented only to person, had rigid neck, incomprehensible speech but followed simple commands, and showed asymmetric left facial droop with greater left arm weakness. A second head CT was unremarkable. Later that day she became unresponsive, required emergency intubation, and was transferred to the MICU. This dramatic deterioration — progressing from walking difficulty to near-coma requiring intubation within 48 hours — was initially evaluated as complicated meningoencephalitis. Multiple antibiotics including vancomycin, ampicillin, and acyclovir were added empirically. Neurology was consulted after LP revealed elevated protein with normal WBC — the pattern pointing away from bacterial meningitis and toward GBS.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, CMP, HIV, anti-GM1/anti-GQ1b ganglioside antibodies, and stool culture / Campylobacter serology if recent diarrhea
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mild leukocytosis / elevated inflammatory markers reflecting antecedent infection; ganglioside antibodies for variant typing; trigger identification (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, HIV)

optimal_actions.action: Order nerve conduction studies and needle EMG (EMG/NCS)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Demyelinating pattern (prolonged DML, conduction block, reduced CV, absent F-waves) consistent with AIDP, or reduced CMAP amplitudes in axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN)

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Albuminocytologic dissociation — elevated protein with cell count <10/μL; may be normal in the first week of illness

useless_tools.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Functional / metabolic brain imaging adds no value in a peripheral demyelinating syndrome.
Cerebrovascular imaging is not indicated in a peripheral neuropathy without focal cerebral signs.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

critical_actions: Mycoplasma serology and PCR (sputum / throat swab) for antecedent confirmation.
Standard antibiotic course for Mycoplasma if active infection persists.
contraindicated_actions: Do not start corticosteroids as monotherapy.
key_reasoning_points: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a recognised GBS trigger (third-most-common after Campylobacter and CMV).
Antecedent confirmation does not change acute management but informs prognosis and counselling.
